Reference: Antràs, Redding and Rossi-Hansberg (2023)

Model Setting

The paper asks how globalization shapes the emergence and severity of pandemics, and how a pandemic in turn feeds back on trade. It combines two mechanisms. First, international trade requires travel: households must meet sellers face to face to source their varieties, so trade and travel both follow a constant elasticity gravity equation that depends on trade and mobility frictions. Second, travel produces human interactions that transmit disease as in a multi-country susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR) model. The difference from existing multigroup SIR models is that the matrix of contacts between countries is an equilibrium outcome of the trade model, so trade costs and travel restrictions determine whether a pandemic occurs and how large it is.

There are four sets of results. (i) Trade-motivated travel creates an epidemiological externality: a global pandemic occurs whenever any single country has a reproduction number based on its domestic interactions above one, so a country that has the disease under control at home cannot escape a pandemic if its trade partners do not. (ii) Lower trade or travel frictions have an ambiguous effect on the global reproduction number, because they raise the total number of interactions and also make households substitute foreign for domestic interactions; with symmetric countries integration makes pandemics more likely and more severe, and with sufficiently different disease environments it can do the opposite. (iii) If the disease kills or lowers the labor supply of the infected, the relative wage of the unhealthy country rises and travel to it falls, a general equilibrium social distancing effect that operates without any individual awareness. (iv) If agents internalize the risk of infection, they cut interactions, and cut foreign interactions by more, so that the ratio of trade to GDP falls sharply early in the pandemic and recovers afterwards. The baseline model has two countries, one sector and no behavioral response; all proofs, the parameter values behind the figures and a long list of extensions (remote trade, a dynamic version in which travel is needed only to start a relationship, many countries and sectors, intermediate inputs, scale economies, imperfect competition) are in the online appendix.

Motivating Evidence

The paper first documents that disease spreads faster to places with stronger trade links, using three diseases: the medieval plague (European cities, 1347 to 1760, first arrival in Messina), the 1957-1958 influenza and COVID-19 (countries, first outbreak in China). The outcome is the log of the arrival time, the time between the first outbreak anywhere and the first outbreak in a location; trade is measured before each outbreak, and all variables are standardized so that coefficients are beta coefficients (robust standard errors in parentheses).

  • Plague: across 1,149 cities, log trade access (the inverse of the distance to the nearest Old World trade route) has a coefficient of −0.219-0.219−0.219 (0.0348), controlling for log distance from Messina, 0.108 (0.0302).

  • Influenza 1957-1958: across 52 countries, log trade with China in 1956 has a coefficient of −0.176-0.176−0.176 (0.1048), with log distance at 0.560 (0.0867).

  • COVID-19: across 172 countries, log trade with China in 2019 has a coefficient of −0.525-0.525−0.525 (0.0742), with log distance at 0.301 (0.0819). Adding the log migrant stock gives −0.238-0.238−0.238 (0.0804) for trade and −0.440-0.440−0.440 (0.0920) for migrants. Adding the log of total arrivals and departures of people between each country and China gives 0.0195 (0.1012) for trade, −0.279-0.279−0.279 (0.0945) for migrants and −0.512-0.512−0.512 (0.1259) for arrivals and departures: trade stops mattering once movements of people are held fixed, as expected if travel is the mechanism.

  • Travel and trade: in a panel of origin-destination-year observations from 1982 to 2019 with pair and year fixed effects (124,597 observations), a 1 percent increase in bilateral trade is associated with a 0.217 percent (0.0111) increase in bilateral air passengers. The elasticity is 0.293 (0.0173) for pairs more than 3,000 kilometers apart and 0.230 (0.0134) when trade is restricted to goods for which air transport is below 20 percent of trade value. Instrumenting trade with bilateral tariffs gives 0.399 (0.1574) with a first-stage F-statistic of 100.8, and the reduced-form coefficient of log air passengers on the log tariff is −1.088-1.088−1.088 (0.3682).

The authors do not claim that these estimates are causal, because in the model trade and travel are jointly determined by the same frictions; they point to quasi-experimental studies (Soderlund 2020; Campante and Yanagizawa-Drott 2018) for causal evidence.

There are two locations, East and West, indexed by iii or jjj, and J\mathcal{J}J denotes the set of countries. Location iii has a continuum of measure LiL_iLi​ of households. Each household produces one differentiated variety with labor, with one unit of labor delivering ZiZ_iZi​ units of goods, and wiw_iwi​ is the wage. There is no intertemporal borrowing, so income equals expenditure. Goods markets are competitive and varieties are sold at marginal cost. Disease Dynamics

The static model is read as a typical day. In the morning the buyer of each household in iii visits niin_{ii}nii​ sellers at home and nijn_{ij}nij​ sellers abroad, while the seller receives niin_{ii}nii​ domestic and njin_{ji}nji​ foreign visitors; buyers do not meet each other. Health status is a household characteristic (transmission within the household is perfect), and households are susceptible, infectious or recovered. In the baseline the disease affects neither labor supply nor mortality, so wages and interactions are constant over time. The population shares SiS_iSi​, IiI_iIi​ and RiR_iRi​ evolve as:

where αi\alpha_iαi​ is the probability that a meeting taking place in country iii between a susceptible and an infectious agent transmits the disease (the contact rate of the location of the meeting) and γi\gamma_iγi​ is the recovery rate of residents of iii. The first term counts domestic infections: a household has 2nii2n_{ii}2nii​ domestic contacts, niin_{ii}nii​ by its buyer and niin_{ii}nii​ by its seller. The second term counts buyers of iii infected while visiting infectious sellers in jjj, with the foreign rate αj\alpha_jαj​. The third counts sellers of iii infected at home by visiting buyers from jjj, with the home rate αi\alpha_iαi​. The parameters differ across countries to reflect culture (mask wearing), administrative capacity (contact tracing) and medical technology. In the closed economy the model is the standard SIR model with βi=2nii\beta_i=2n_{ii}βi​=2nii​ and domestic reproduction number R0i=βi/γi\mathcal{R}_{0i}=\beta_i/\gamma_iR0i​=βi​/γi​ as written in the paper (which leaves the factor αi\alpha_iαi​ implicit here; elsewhere the domestic number is 2αinii/γi2\alpha_in_{ii}/\gamma_i2αi​nii​/γi​): an epidemic occurs if and only if it exceeds one.

The proof applies results for multigroup SIR models (Hethcote 1978; Magal, Ousmane and Webb 2016), taking the contact matrix as given. After a small initial infection with R0>1\mathcal{R}_0>1R0​>1, worldwide infections rise for a time and then vanish. The two equations are the two-country version of the final-size equation of the SIR model: the log of the surviving susceptible share equals minus the cumulative force of infection, which sums domestic and cross-border exposure to all those ever infected. Total differentiation shows that Si(∞)S_i(\infty)Si​(∞) and Sj(∞)S_j(\infty)Sj​(∞) are decreasing in each of niin_{ii}nii​, njjn_{jj}njj​, nijn_{ij}nij​ and njin_{ji}nji​, so the comparative statics of interactions translate into comparative statics of the size of the pandemic.

Epidemiological Externality

Since R0\mathcal{R}_0R0​ is nondecreasing in nijn_{ij}nij​ and njin_{ji}nji​:

R0≥R0∣nij=nji=0=max⁡{2αiniiγi,2αjnjjγj}(17)\mathcal{R}_0\geq\left.\mathcal{R}_0\right|_{n_{ij}=n_{ji}=0}=\max\left\{\frac{2\alpha_in_{ii}}{\gamma_i},\frac{2\alpha_jn_{jj}}{\gamma_j}\right\} \tag{17}R0​≥R0​∣nij​=nji​=0​=max{γi​2αi​nii​​,γj​2αj​njj​​}(17)

Even if one country has a domestic reproduction number below one, it necessarily takes part in a global pandemic if there is positive trade and the other country does not have the disease under control. With N≥2N\geq2N≥2 countries and arbitrary asymmetries, a sufficient condition for a pandemic is that any one country has a domestic reproduction number above one. The qualification is that the domestic interactions in this bound are those of the open economy, which are lower than in autarky and fall with the number of trade partners, so the bound does not by itself say that openness makes pandemics more likely. In the numerical illustration two identical countries start with α1=α2=0.04\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0.04α1​=α2​=0.04, which gives R0=0.75\mathcal{R}_0=0.75R0​=0.75 and open-economy domestic reproduction numbers of 0.46, so an initial infection dies out. Raising α2\alpha_2α2​ alone from 0.04 to 0.10 raises R0\mathcal{R}_0R0​ monotonically from 0.75 to 1.46; once it passes one, both countries experience increasingly severe pandemics although nothing changes in country 1. When the timing of the first waves differs strongly across countries and the countries are sufficiently different in size, the model also generates multiple waves of infection; otherwise the pandemic is synchronized with a single peak.

Trade Integration and Pandemics

Integration acts through two channels: it raises total interactions (with symmetric countries), which promotes diffusion, and it shifts interactions from home to abroad, which helps or hurts depending on the disease environments (αi\alpha_iαi​, αj\alpha_jαj​, γi\gamma_iγi​, γj\gamma_jγj​). In a fully symmetric world, with ndom≡nii=njjn_{dom}\equiv n_{ii}=n_{jj}ndom​≡nii​=njj​, nfor≡nij=njin_{for}\equiv n_{ij}=n_{ji}nfor​≡nij​=nji​, αi=αj=α\alpha_i=\alpha_j=\alphaαi​=αj​=α and γi=γj=γ\gamma_i=\gamma_j=\gammaγi​=γj​=γ:

R0=2α(ndom+nfor)γ(18)\mathcal{R}_0=\frac{2\alpha\left(n_{dom}+n_{for}\right)}{\gamma} \tag{18}R0​=γ2α(ndom​+nfor​)​(18)

and the common steady-state share of susceptibles solves:

ln⁡Si(∞)=−2α(ndom+nfor)γ[1−Si(∞)](19)\ln S_i(\infty)=-\frac{2\alpha\left(n_{dom}+n_{for}\right)}{\gamma}\left[1-S_i(\infty)\right] \tag{19}lnSi​(∞)=−γ2α(ndom​+nfor​)​[1−Si​(∞)](19)

Proposition 2. Suppose countries are symmetric (Li=LL_i=LLi​=L, Zi=ZZ_i=ZZi​=Z, Υij=Υ\Upsilon_{ij}=\UpsilonΥij​=Υ, αi=α\alpha_i=\alphaαi​=α, γi=γ\gamma_i=\gammaγi​=γ). Then a decline in any symmetric international trade friction (i) increases R0\mathcal{R}_0R0​, which shrinks the range of parameters for which the pandemic-free equilibrium is stable, and (ii) increases the share of each country's population that becomes infected when R0>1\mathcal{R}_0>1R0​>1. The proof is immediate: with symmetry only total interactions matter, because a contact transmits equally at home and abroad, and total interactions rise when frictions fall. A numerical example with α1=0.04\alpha_1=0.04α1​=0.04 and α2=0.07\alpha_2=0.07α2​=0.07 shows that the result survives moderate asymmetry: starting from t12=t21=μ12=μ21=1t_{12}=t_{21}=\mu_{12}=\mu_{21}=1t12​=t21​=μ12​=μ21​=1, where both countries have a pandemic, raising tariffs or travel restrictions lowers R0\mathcal{R}_0R0​ smoothly and reduces cumulative infections until the pandemic disappears.

The opposite case arises when disease environments differ strongly. Suppose country jjj is much safer, with very low αj\alpha_jαj​ and very high γj\gamma_jγj​. In the limit αj→0\alpha_j\rightarrow0αj​→0, the condition R0<1\mathcal{R}_0<1R0​<1 becomes:

2αiniiγi+1γj(αinji)2γi<1(20)\frac{2\alpha_in_{ii}}{\gamma_i}+\frac{1}{\gamma_j}\frac{\left(\alpha_in_{ji}\right)^2}{\gamma_i}<1 \tag{20}γi​2αi​nii​​+γj​1​γi​(αi​nji​)2​<1(20)

For high γj\gamma_jγj​ the second term is small, so the fall in niin_{ii}nii​ caused by lower international barriers relaxes the condition even though njin_{ji}nji​ rises. Proposition 3. When the contagion rate αi\alpha_iαi​ and the recovery rate γi\gamma_iγi​ vary sufficiently across countries, a decline in any international trade friction (i) decreases R0\mathcal{R}_0R0​, which enlarges the range of parameters for which the pandemic-free equilibrium is stable, and (ii) when R0>1\mathcal{R}_0>1R0​>1, reduces the share of the population of the high-risk country (high αi\alpha_iαi​, low γi\gamma_iγi​) that becomes infected, and may also reduce that share in the low-risk country. The intuition is dilution: openness leads residents of the high-risk country to replace risky domestic meetings with meetings in the safe country, and the fall in their domestic interactions keeps the disease in check even if their total interactions rise. In the illustration with α1=0.008\alpha_1=0.008α1​=0.008 and α2=0.052\alpha_2=0.052α2​=0.052 (and ccc lowered to 0.1 and ϕ\phiϕ to 1.5), there is no pandemic without frictions, and raising tariffs or travel restrictions raises R0\mathcal{R}_0R0​ above one. Higher frictions always worsen the pandemic in the risky country 2. In the safe country 1 they first worsen it and only very high frictions isolate it; in autarky country 1 avoids the pandemic entirely, at a large cost in the income of both countries. The authors note that such large differences may be rare in practice, but cite evidence that domestic travel bans can raise cumulative infections by trapping people in hot spots (Burlig, Sudarshan and Schlauch 2021) and that localized lockdowns are undermined by spillovers from neighbors (Li, Undurraga and Zubizarreta 2022).

Deaths and General Equilibrium Social Distancing

Now infected agents die at rate ηi\eta_iηi​ and recover at rate γi\gamma_iγi​, both determined by the country of residence, while agents remain unaware of the source of infection and do not change their behavior. With DiD_iDi​ the share of dead households:

S˙i=−2nii(w)αiSiIi−[nij(w)αj+nji(w)αi]SiIjI˙i=2nii(w)αiSiIi+[nij(w)αj+nji(w)αi]SiIj−(γi+ηi)IiR˙i=γiIiD˙i=ηiIi(21)\begin{aligned} \dot{S}_i&=-2n_{ii}\left(\mathbf{w}\right)\alpha_iS_iI_i-\left[n_{ij}\left(\mathbf{w}\right)\alpha_j+n_{ji}\left(\mathbf{w}\right)\alpha_i\right]S_iI_j\\ \dot{I}_i&=2n_{ii}\left(\mathbf{w}\right)\alpha_iS_iI_i+\left[n_{ij}\left(\mathbf{w}\right)\alpha_j+n_{ji}\left(\mathbf{w}\right)\alpha_i\right]S_iI_j-\left(\gamma_i+\eta_i\right)I_i\\ \dot{R}_i&=\gamma_iI_i\\ \dot{D}_i&=\eta_iI_i \end{aligned} \tag{21}S˙i​I˙i​R˙i​D˙i​​=−2nii​(w)αi​Si​Ii​−[nij​(w)αj​+nji​(w)αi​]Si​Ij​=2nii​(w)αi​Si​Ii​+[nij​(w)αj​+nji​(w)αi​]Si​Ij​−(γi​+ηi​)Ii​=γi​Ii​=ηi​Ii​​(21)

Interactions now depend on the wage vector, which changes over the pandemic because deaths change labor supply. Wages solve the goods market clearing condition:

∑j∈Jπji(w)wj(1−Dj)Lj=wi(1−Di)Li(22)\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\pi_{ji}\left(\mathbf{w}\right)w_j\left(1-D_j\right)L_j=w_i\left(1-D_i\right)L_i \tag{22}j∈J∑​πji​(w)wj​(1−Dj​)Lj​=wi​(1−Di​)Li​(22)

with trade shares and interactions given by the same expressions as before. The system is continuous in ηi\eta_iηi​ and reduces to the baseline at ηi=0\eta_i=0ηi​=0, so all earlier results hold for sufficiently small death rates. Deaths lower a country's labor supply, which changes its relative wage (a terms of trade effect) and the measure of varieties it produces; in an interior equilibrium the relative wage summarizes all general equilibrium effects. Proposition 4. If country jjj experiences more deaths than country iii, the resulting change in relative wages wj/wiw_j/w_iwj​/wi​ leads country iii to reduce its interactions with country jjj and increase its interactions with itself. The mechanism is a price effect: scarcer labor in jjj raises wj/wiw_j/w_iwj​/wi​, the varieties of jjj become more expensive, and by the gravity equation buyers from both countries source fewer of them. The elasticity of a country's relative wage with respect to its own population is larger in absolute value when the trade elasticity is smaller and when the country earns a smaller share of its income at home; it is bounded by one in absolute value. Because the waves of infection can be staggered, the identity of the country with more deaths, and hence the direction of the effect, can change during the pandemic. Deaths also add a welfare channel for trade policy: aggregate real income wiLi/Piw_iL_i/P_iwi​Li​/Pi​ and aggregate welfare WiLiW_iL_iWi​Li​ move with population, and near R0=1\mathcal{R}_0=1R0​=1 deaths respond strongly to frictions.

In the illustration country 1 has a death rate among the infected of 1 percent (η1/(η1+γ1)=0.01\eta_1/\left(\eta_1+\gamma_1\right)=0.01η1​/(η1​+γ1​)=0.01) and country 2 of 50 percent (η2/(η2+γ2)=0.50\eta_2/\left(\eta_2+\gamma_2\right)=0.50η2​/(η2​+γ2​)=0.50), with otherwise symmetric countries. About 6 percent of the population of country 2 dies, yet its relative wage rises by only 0.5 percent, because demand and the set of varieties fall together with labor supply. Both countries tilt purchases towards the varieties of country 1; both source fewer varieties in total and both price indices rise, more in country 2. Real income per capita falls in country 1 and rises in country 2, where aggregate real income nevertheless falls. As supporting evidence, the paper cites the rise in real wages after the Black Death, which reduced Europe's population by around one third, and faster manufacturing wage growth from 1914 to 1919 in US states and cities with higher influenza mortality (Garrett 2009).

Reduced Labor Supply of the Infected

Suppose in addition that infected agents supply only 1−ςi>01-\varsigma_i>01−ςi​>0 units of labor and isolate when they do not work, so that their interactions are proportional to their labor supply. The laws of motion for susceptibles and infected become:

with the equations for RiR_iRi​ and DiD_iDi​ unchanged, and goods market clearing becomes:

∑j∈Jπji(w)wj(1−Dj−ςjIj)Lj=wi(1−Di−ςiIi)Li(24)\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\pi_{ji}\left(\mathbf{w}\right)w_j\left(1-D_j-\varsigma_jI_j\right)L_j=w_i\left(1-D_i-\varsigma_iI_i\right)L_i \tag{24}j∈J∑​πji​(w)wj​(1−Dj​−ςj​Ij​)Lj​=wi​(1−Di​−ςi​Ii​)Li​(24)

The term Liwf≡(1−Di−ςiIi)LiL_i^{wf}\equiv\left(1-D_i-\varsigma_iI_i\right)L_iLiwf​≡(1−Di​−ςi​Ii​)Li​ is the effective labor supply of country iii. A higher ςi\varsigma_iςi​ has two effects. Directly, it flattens the infection curve and lowers total infections, since the infected meet fewer people; in the limit ςi=1\varsigma_i=1ςi​=1 in all countries there is no pandemic. Through general equilibrium, high current infections lower a country's labor supply and raise its relative wage, which diverts interactions away from it. Unlike deaths, this effect is temporary and follows the relative number of currently infected, so it is richest when the waves are not synchronized. Repeating the previous example with ςi\varsigma_iςi​ between 0 and 0.05, the dominant effect is the smaller pandemic, which also weakens the labor supply and relative wage effects. In an appendix variant where the infected are less productive but do not isolate, the relative wage effect alone lowers the peak of infections in both countries.

Behavioral Responses

Finally, agents know that infection can kill and adjust their interactions. Following Farboodi, Jarosch and Shimer (2021), all infections are asymptomatic: a household does not observe its own health status and holds rational beliefs si(t)s_i(t)si​(t), ii(t)i_i(t)ii​(t) and ki(t)k_i(t)ki​(t) about being susceptible, infected or dead, the last denoted kik_iki​ to avoid confusion with distance. Given ii(0)i_i(0)ii​(0), si(0)s_i(0)si​(0) and ki(0)=0k_i(0)=0ki​(0)=0, the household chooses paths of interactions at date zero, with commitment:

together with transversality conditions that set the limit of each costate times its state to zero. The costate equation for the infected state contains no term from the infection hazard, which is consistent with treating the infection shares inside the braces as aggregate rates that the household takes as given, although the problem is written with lower-case letters. In equilibrium beliefs equal population shares, ii(t)=Ii(t)i_i(t)=I_i(t)ii​(t)=Ii​(t), si(t)=Si(t)s_i(t)=S_i(t)si​(t)=Si​(t) and ki(t)=Di(t)k_i(t)=D_i(t)ki​(t)=Di​(t), and wages clear the goods market with labor supply [1−Di(t)]Li\left[1-D_i(t)\right]L_i[1−Di​(t)]Li​ at each date. The right-hand side of the optimality condition is the expected cost of one more meeting: the probability of being susceptible, times the probability that the meeting infects, times the loss in value from moving from the susceptible to the infected state.

Lemma 1. Along the transition path θis(t)−θii(t)≥0\theta_i^s(t)-\theta_i^i(t)\geq0θis​(t)−θii​(t)≥0 for all ttt, which implies:

∂Qi(nii(t),nij(t))∂nij(t)>∂Ci(nii(t),nij(t))∂nij(t)as long asIj(t)>0(28)\frac{\partial Q_i\left(n_{ii}(t),n_{ij}(t)\right)}{\partial n_{ij}(t)}>\frac{\partial C_i\left(n_{ii}(t),n_{ij}(t)\right)}{\partial n_{ij}(t)}\quad\text{as long as}\quad I_j(t)>0 \tag{28}∂nij​(t)∂Qi​(nii​(t),nij​(t))​>∂nij​(t)∂Ci​(nii​(t),nij​(t))​as long asIj​(t)>0(28)

Being susceptible is worth at least as much as being infected, so households reduce interactions until marginal utility exceeds marginal cost: this is individual-level social distancing. Substituting the functional forms, the optimality condition becomes:

1σ−11nijnijqijσ−1σ∑ℓ∈Jniℓqiℓσ−1σQi=1nijcμijdijρnijϕ+[θis(t)−θii(t)]si(t)αjIj(t)[1−Di(t)]e−ξt(29)\frac{1}{\sigma-1}\frac{1}{n_{ij}}\frac{n_{ij}q_{ij}^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\sigma}}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{J}}n_{i\ell}q_{i\ell}^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\sigma}}}Q_i=\frac{1}{n_{ij}}c\mu_{ij}d_{ij}^{\rho}n_{ij}^{\phi}+\frac{\left[\theta_i^s(t)-\theta_i^i(t)\right]s_i(t)\alpha_jI_j(t)}{\left[1-D_i(t)\right]e^{-\xi t}} \tag{29}σ−11​nij​1​∑ℓ∈J​niℓ​qiℓσσ−1​​nij​qijσσ−1​​​Qi​=nij​1​cμij​dijρ​nijϕ​+[1−Di​(t)]e−ξt[θis​(t)−θii​(t)]si​(t)αj​Ij​(t)​(29)

where the left-hand side is the marginal utility of interactions, the first term on the right is their marginal cost and the second is the wedge created by the threat of infection. (The paper's display omits the factor 1/(σ−1)1/\left(\sigma-1\right)1/(σ−1) on the left-hand side, which comes from differentiating the static objective; the argument does not depend on it.) Foreign varieties are generically a smaller share of the consumption index than domestic ones, so the left-hand side is smaller for i≠ji\neq ji=j and a larger proportional cut in nijn_{ij}nij​ is needed to open a given wedge. The pandemic therefore reduces foreign interactions by more than domestic ones, and trade falls relative to output. When ηi=0\eta_i=0ηi​=0 the costates play no role and the model returns to the baseline; by continuity all baseline results hold for small ηi\eta_iηi​. Agents' choices are privately optimal but not socially optimal, because each household ignores that its own interactions raise the infection risk of others; this infection externality is pointed out, and the planner's problem is left for future work. Since the wedge vanishes when Ii(t)=Ij(t)=0I_i(t)=I_j(t)=0Ii​(t)=Ij​(t)=0, interactions and trade return to their pre-pandemic levels as soon as the pandemic ends, and an appendix extension with symmetric adjustment costs still gives a rapid V-shaped recovery.

Solution Method and Numerical Illustration

The paper does not estimate or calibrate the model to data: the figures are numerical illustrations with parameter values listed in the online appendix, and the main text reports only the values varied in each exercise. The algorithms are also described there. With behavioral responses the equilibrium is computed by a backward shooting algorithm: guess the shares of deaths and infections far in the future when the pandemic is over, solve the dynamic path backward and forward, and iterate until the solution is consistent with the guess. With asymmetric countries the path is highly sensitive to the relative value of final infections even when their level is close to zero, which makes it hard to solve the model for many parameter values or more countries.

  • Symmetric countries: with αi=0.1\alpha_i=0.1αi​=0.1, γi+ηi=0.2\gamma_i+\eta_i=0.2γi​+ηi​=0.2 and a death rate among the infected of ηi/(ηi+γi)=0.0062\eta_i/\left(\eta_i+\gamma_i\right)=0.0062ηi​/(ηi​+γi​)=0.0062 (0.62 percent), compared with half that rate (0.003) and with no behavioral response, the response flattens the curve: the peak and cumulative infections are lower, the pandemic lasts longer, and total deaths are delayed and reduced, more so the higher the death rate. The cost is fewer varieties, a higher price index and lower real income. The ratio of trade to GDP (imports plus exports over GDP) falls from about 0.45 to less than 0.25 with a death rate of 0.3 percent and to 0.17 with 0.62 percent.

  • Role of frictions: higher trade or mobility frictions lower the level of interactions and of trade openness, which dampens the absolute size of the behavioral response, and shift more of the adjustment to domestic interactions. With 10 percent trade frictions (t12=t21=1.1t_{12}=t_{21}=1.1t12​=t21​=1.1) trade falls essentially to zero in the most severe phase. For the parameter values considered, higher frictions also reduce total deaths.

  • Asymmetric mortality: country 1 has a mortality rate of 0.3 percent and country 2 of 0.62 percent. The response is stronger in country 2, whose infection curve is flatter. Country 1 ends with about 10 percent more total infections but only about half the deaths. It is the more dangerous destination early on and the safer one later, because it reaches herd immunity sooner. Its relative wage first falls, as demand shifts away from its varieties, then recovers and rises temporarily above one before returning to one. The demand effect of behavioral responses thus dominates and reverses the labor supply effect of the previous extension, under which the country with more deaths has the higher relative wage. Trade openness falls sharply, most in country 2. Compared with a symmetric world with the average mortality rate of 0.46 percent, the world infection curve is marginally flatter, and trade openness falls by more initially and is higher later.

  • Evidence: world trade fell faster than world production early in the COVID-19 pandemic and then recovered. Goolsbee and Syverson (2021) find that most of a 60 percentage point fall in consumer traffic reflected individual behavior, with government restrictions contributing only around 7 percent. Akerman et al. (2022) find that Swedish firms exporting to more heavily affected destinations saw larger falls in exports, exceeding the falls in their total revenue.

This is an assumed functional form, the primitive that creates an extensive margin of trade. It gives the utility cost that a household of iii bears when its buyer travels to secure nijn_{ij}nij​ varieties from location jjj. The cost is measured in units of utility (it is subtracted from the consumption index in equation (2)), not in goods or labor, so it does not appear in the budget constraint (3) and uses no resources.

The terms are: c>0c>0c>0, a common shifter; μij≥1\mu_{ij}\geq1μij​≥1, the travel restriction that country jjj imposes on visitors from iii; dij≥1d_{ij}\geq1dij​≥1, distance, with elasticity ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0; and ϕ>1\phi>1ϕ>1, the elasticity of the cost with respect to the number of varieties. The marginal cost and its elasticity are

∂cij∂nij=cμij(dij)ρ(nij)ϕ−1,∂ln⁡(∂cij/∂nij)∂ln⁡nij=ϕ−1>0\frac{\partial c_{ij}}{\partial n_{ij}}=c\mu_{ij}\left(d_{ij}\right)^{\rho}\left(n_{ij}\right)^{\phi-1},\qquad\frac{\partial\ln\left(\partial c_{ij}/\partial n_{ij}\right)}{\partial\ln n_{ij}}=\phi-1>0∂nij​∂cij​​=cμij​(dij​)ρ(nij​)ϕ−1,∂lnnij​∂ln(∂cij​/∂nij​)​=ϕ−1>0

The division by ϕ\phiϕ is a normalization that makes the marginal cost free of ϕ\phiϕ as a multiplicative constant. Convexity (ϕ>1\phi>1ϕ>1) is what delivers an interior number of varieties: the marginal gain from one more variety is weighed against a rising marginal travel cost. The inverse 1/(ϕ−1)1/\left(\phi-1\right)1/(ϕ−1) is the elasticity of the number of meetings with respect to the net gain from a meeting, and it appears as an exponent throughout the gravity equations (7) and (8). As ϕ→∞\phi\rightarrow\inftyϕ→∞ the number of varieties stops responding and the model returns to a standard Armington model.

The cost is additively separable across destinations, so the choice of nijn_{ij}nij​ interacts with niin_{ii}nii​ only through the price index. Two instruments of policy are kept apart: μij\mu_{ij}μij​ acts on people (this equation) and tijt_{ij}tij​ acts on goods (through τij\tau_{ij}τij​). A numerical illustration: with ϕ=2\phi=2ϕ=2 the cost is quadratic, and doubling μij\mu_{ij}μij​ halves the number of meetings for a given marginal gain.

This is the definition of the household's problem, from which equations (4) to (7) are derived. The objective has two parts.

The first is a CES consumption index over the varieties actually sourced. The integral runs from 000 to nijn_{ij}nij​, so the measure of varieties from each origin is a choice variable and not a primitive; qij(k)q_{ij}(k)qij​(k) is the quantity of variety kkk from jjj and σ>1\sigma>1σ>1 is the elasticity of substitution. Because σ>1\sigma>1σ>1 the household values variety. If it consumes the same quantity qqq of a measure nnn of varieties, the index is

[nqσ−1σ]σσ−1=nσσ−1q\left[nq^{\frac{\sigma-1}{\sigma}}\right]^{\frac{\sigma}{\sigma-1}}=n^{\frac{\sigma}{\sigma-1}}q[nqσσ−1​]σ−1σ​=nσ−1σ​q

which rises more than proportionally with nnn. This love of variety is the only reason to travel.

The second part is the sum over destinations of the travel cost in equation (1), in utility units. The household therefore trades off more variety against the disutility of the buyer's time away from home.

The maximization is over the measures niin_{ii}nii​ and nijn_{ij}nij​ and over the quantity schedules, subject to the budget constraint (3). The problem can be solved in two stages: for given measures, choose quantities (this gives the CES demand (4) and the price index (5)); then choose the measures (this gives the reduced problem (6) and the gravity equation (7)). The value WiW_iWi​ is the welfare of a household of iii and is used later for the welfare effects of frictions and of deaths. Since each sourced variety requires one face-to-face meeting, the chosen nijn_{ij}nij​ is also the number of contacts that enters the disease dynamics in equation (13).

This is the household's budget constraint. The left-hand side is total spending: for each origin jjj, the price pij(k)p_{ij}(k)pij​(k) paid in iii for variety kkk of jjj times the quantity qij(k)q_{ij}(k)qij​(k), added over the nijn_{ij}nij​ varieties sourced there and over origins. The right-hand side is income. A household supplies one unit of labor, earns the wage wiw_iwi​, and there are no profits because goods markets are competitive with constant returns; there is no borrowing or lending, so income equals spending in every period.

Three features matter for what follows. First, travel costs do not enter: they are utility costs (equation (1)), so the whole income is spent on goods. Second, prices are pinned down by technology and trade costs. The equation is log-linear in a bilateral friction term, an origin term (wj/Zjw_j/Z_jwj​/Zj​) and destination terms (wiw_iwi​, PiP_iPi​), which is the structure of a gravity equation. The laws of motion follow from counting the meetings of a susceptible household of iii during a day and applying the law of large numbers. A household has two members who meet other people: its buyer and its seller. The four sources of infection are as follows.

The buyer visits niin_{ii}nii​ domestic sellers. Each is infectious with probability IiI_iIi​ (varieties are chosen at random), and a meeting located in iii transmits with probability αi\alpha_iαi​, so the hazard is niiαiIin_{ii}\alpha_iI_inii​αi​Ii​. Finally the seller receives visiting buyers from jjj, each infectious with probability IjI_jIj​, in meetings located in iii: hazard njiαiIjn_{ji}\alpha_iI_jnji​αi​Ij​. This is the definition of the household's dynamic problem in the behavioral extension. Nothing is derived here; equations (26) and (27) are its optimality conditions.

The objective is discounted expected utility. Infection itself has no direct utility cost and does not reduce income in this version; it matters only because it may lead to death.

The constraints are the laws of motion of the household's beliefs about its own health, which mirror the aggregate system (21) at the individual level. All infections are asymptomatic, so the household never learns its status and cannot condition its behavior on it; it tracks the probabilities sis_isi​, iii_iii​ and kik_iki​. This extra term has no economic meaning: a household's own probability of being infected does not raise its own risk of catching the disease, which depends on how many of the people it meets are infectious. The correct specification therefore has the aggregate shares Ii(t)I_i(t)Ii​(t) and Ij(t)I_j(t)Ij​(t) in the hazard, taken as given, and under it the printed costate equation without a hazard term is the correct one. Why the costates are ordered. The costate equations (27) show the logic. The shadow value of death is negative, θik(t)=−∫t∞[Qi−Ci]e−ξτdτ<0\theta_i^k(t)=-\int_t^{\infty}\left[Q_i-C_i\right]e^{-\xi\tau}d\tau<0θik​(t)=−∫t∞​[Qi​−Ci​]e−ξτdτ<0. The qualitative argument is unaffected, since the constant is common to all origins. The left-hand side is proportional to the share of origin jjj in the consumption index per variety sourced, and the wedge for domestic meetings is the same expression with αiIi(t)\alpha_iI_i(t)αi​Ii​(t) in place of αjIj(t)\alpha_jI_j(t)αj​Ij​(t). For a given wedge the adjustment in nijn_{ij}nij​ needed to raise the net marginal gain is larger where the marginal utility and marginal cost are low to begin with, which is the case for foreign varieties, so foreign interactions fall proportionally more and trade falls relative to output. When Ij(t)=0I_j(t)=0Ij​(t)=0 the wedge is zero and interactions return to their static values.
